..
Issued at 246 AM EDT Wed Aug 12 2026

GOES-East Nighttime Microphysics RGB imagery shows a few tall 
thunderstorms south of the state line, though one of the weaker 
cells appears to be tracking towards the Menominee/Marinette metro. 
While a few lightning strikes have been sparsely observed, the 
impacts should be low as the storm continues to be weak among a 
stabilized nighttime surface layer and absent of much synoptic 
forcing or shearing mechanism. Also evident on the RGB is some 
scattered midlevel cumulus and some patches of low stratus/fog that 
are causing some vis restrictions at ESC, IWD, and CMX airports this 
morning. While temperatures will continue to fall towards the dew 
point (already matching it at some locations), the model signatures 
for fog are mixed. Thus, maintaining the ongoing expectation of 
patches to areas of fog, some dense, but not enough confidence to 
issue an advisory (though if coverage increases around the commute 
times, may issue an SPS). 

RAP analysis aloft shows general northwesterly flow extending from 
the Atlantic Seaboard to the lee of the Canadian Rockies. Ridging 
extends across much of the southern tier of the US (highest 500mb 
heights over the Gulf Coast but the northern extent of the ridge 
axis is over the US Rockies). Meanwhile a closed low remains 
over Hudson Bay and a trough is over the Pacific Northwest. The 
latter trough will provide the best mechanism to progress the 
weather pattern, though progress will have to wait for later in 
the week as today looks to be yet another day of northwest flow 
aloft leading to low confidence in diurnally-boosted 
showers/thunderstorms. Ignoring the CAMs that do not have a good
handle on ongoing thunderstorms in Wisconsin, the most 
aggressive CAM in convective initiation is the 00Z WRF ARW, 
which shows weak thunderstorms forming at the confluence of lake
breeze boundaries at 18Z, with the remainder of the CAMs 
showing weak and isolated showers in the proceeding hours. 
Similar to yesterday, the UP lacks synoptic support for forcing 
and has mostly unidirectional, weak shear (especially in the 
lowest ~250mb where wind speeds only rarely exceed 20 kt). 
SBCAPE is also similar to yesterday, with a HREF mean of up to 
500 J/kg, but the spread from minimum to maximum in the ensemble
is 1000+ J/kg.

Thursday and Friday, the kicking trough will first kick ridging from 
over the Rockies and Plains to be over the Midwest and Great Lakes. 
This will lead to rising surface pressure and mostly dry conditions 
for virtually all of the UP Thursday and Friday, though temperatures 
in the 70s look to be around seasonal to even cooler-than-normal. 
The exception to the dry conditions Thursday would be the scenario 
presented by a few of the CAMs where the messy remnants of MCS 
structures in Minnesota move over the UP, though even if this
does occur (less than 50% chance) impacts will be low as these 
are unlikely to have enough support or buoyancy to sustain as 
thunderstorms and even the 90th percentile of HREF 24hr QPF is a
tenth to a quarter inch for a reasonable wettest case scenario.

The aforementioned kicking trough arrives over the UP Saturday. 
Unfortunately and unsurprisingly, spread in the track and depth of 
this trough passage remains high. At the same time as the trough 
arrives, ridging builds over the Southeast, allowing for ensembles 
to have a spread of solutions regarding how this trough fares 
against either a weaker or stronger Southeast ridge. Current LREF 
chances of a wetting rain (around a tenth of an inch/24hr) is around 
50-65% by Sunday morning. Thunderstorms are uncertain as well, 
though the LREF mean SBCAPE by 00Z Sunday being 100 or less J/kg is 
not an encouraging sign for those looking forward to a rumble of 
thunder. While there is understandable spread on the pattern that 
follows, it is generally expected that by Sunday evening and through 
Monday night, ridging resumes in the wake of the trough. Next 
Tuesday looking to resume the ongoing pattern of weak precip signals 
in persistent NWerly flow, unless the ensembles can coalesce around 
the global deterministic models which each have their own idea of 
how the closed low aloft over Hudson Bay may gyrate south enough 
into northern Ontario to bring decent enough PVA to support showers 
and storms.
